bipartite.relationship_type: wordplay-preface reworked into a rhetorical simile/wish
bipartite.note: Dickens inverts the original structure: he opens with the wish itself ('if thou'rt as fair... deign my hut to grace') then reworks the sanekazura/Osakayama material as a closing simile for secrecy ('as secret be... as is the trace of Sanekads'ra mid Osaka-yama's forests hid'). This collapses the jokotoba-driven pivot into a straightforward simile structure — the kami material is displaced to the end and subordinated grammatically to the shimo's wish, rather than functioning as a name-driven preface that generates the wish. The bipartite logic (preface generating pivot generating wish) is lost; instead we get wish-then-simile, a different but coherent rhetorical shape.

kakekotoba_handling.note: Osaka-yama is kept as a proper place name (transliterated), which preserves the literal toponym reading; the embedded 'meeting hill' pun (逢ふ坂) is not activated or hinted at in English — the translator treats it purely as geography providing atmospheric cover ('forests hid'), so the secondary meaning is lost.

Transliterated as a plant name only ('Sanekads'ra'), used as the vehicle of a simile for secrecy/hiddenness. The さ寝 (sleeping together) pun and the 繰る (drawing in) association are not rendered; it functions merely as an exotic plant name hidden in forests, losing the erotic and pivot-generating double meaning entirely.

There is no word in the translation that plays on 来る/繰る; the wish for the beloved to come is rendered plainly as 'deign my hut to grace' with no vine-pulling or coming-pivot preserved, and the vine image is repurposed only as a simile for secrecy rather than as the source of the 'come' pivot.

kigo_handling.note: Source analysis marks kigo as 'none' — no season is truly at stake in the original. Dickens' 'forests hid' adds a woodland/hidden atmosphere but this is not tied to any seasonal signal in the source and does not constitute a seasonal image; it's simply invented scenic cover for the secrecy conceit.

entries.content_summary: If thou'rt as fair as rumour thee (paraphrase of 人にしられで / conditional address to beloved, drawing on 'if it lives up to its name' logic but transposed to beauty)
Doth paint, O deign my hut to grace — wish for beloved to come, rendered as invitation
And may thy path as secret be — the 'unknown to others' (人にしられで) wish
To human eye — continues 'unknown to people' theme
as is the trace / Of Sanekads'ra — the sanekazura vine image reused as simile vehicle
'mid Osaka-yama's forests hid — Osakayama reused as simile setting, providing 'hidden' quality

line_mapping.structural_note: Dickens restructures the whole poem as a single extended sentence: a conditional wish (kami of shimo, i.e. the 'come to me' desire) is stated first, then justified/illustrated by a simile drawn from the kami's proper-noun material (Osakayama, sanekazura) recast as an image of hiddenness. This is a significant inversion of the source's build-up-then-pivot structure into a claim-then-illustration structure.

Dickens.translator_strategy: Dickens sacrifices the wordplay entirely, converting the jokotoba's name-puns into a simple end-of-poem simile of concealment while foregrounding a Victorian courtly-love address ('if thou'rt as fair as rumour') that has no direct source equivalent, prioritizing rhymed English verse elegance over rhetorical fidelity.

bipartite.note: The translator has restructured the poem as a single rhetorical question ('Is there no way to come as secret') that fuses the shimo's wish (くる/しられで) into line 1, then retroactively supplies the kami material (Osaka mountain, sanekazura vine) as a simile clause justifying the wish, ending with an exclamatory aside ('Oh, reel of the vine!') that stands in for the pivot word くる/繰る. This inverts the original order (kami preface then shimo wish) into wish-first-then-image, and collapses the jokotoba's separate wordplay logic into a direct simile ('as secret as the trace of...'), losing the associative/pivot structure entirely.

kakekotoba_handling.note: Rendered simply as the place name with no hint of 逢ふ (meeting) wordplay; the 'secret meeting' sense is expressed elsewhere in the poem (line 1) but not tied to this place name itself.
Transliterated as a botanical name; the さ寝 (sleeping together) pun is not activated in English, though the surrounding romantic context implies intimacy indirectly.

The translator invents an exclamatory apostrophe 'Oh, reel of the vine!' which evokes the drawing/pulling sense (繰る) via 'reel' but detaches it from the literal 来る (to come), which was already expressed in line 1 as 'come.' The pivot's simultaneity (one word carrying both senses at once) is split into two separate lines/moments rather than fused.

kigo_handling.note: No seasonal atmosphere is introduced or implied; the vine is treated purely as a botanical/wordplay image tied to secrecy and romance, consistent with the source's own lack of seasonal marking.

entries.content_summary: The wish/question 'is there no way to come secretly' — corresponds to shimo's 人にしられで くるよしもがな, moved to the front.
The simile 'as the trace of a sanekatsura vine' — corresponds to kami's さねかづら.
'Of the Osaka mountain' completing the simile, referencing 名にしおはば逢坂山 as the source of the vine/place name.
Exclamatory aside 'Oh, reel of the vine!' isolating the 繰る (draw/reel) sense of くる as a separate apostrophe.

line_mapping.structural_note: The translator inverts kami/shimo order, placing the shimo's wish first as a rhetorical question, then supplying the kami's place-name/vine imagery as the grounds for the simile, and finally isolating the kakekotoba pivot (くる) as a standalone exclamation — a significant restructuring that trades the original's forward-building jokotoba logic for a question-then-justification-then-aside structure.

Noguchi.translator_strategy: Noguchi prioritizes a vivid, compact English question-and-exclamation structure over literal ku-by-ku fidelity, converting the jokotoba's associative name-play into an explicit simile ('as secret as...') and isolating the くる/繰る pun as a final poetic apostrophe rather than fusing its double meaning into one word.

bipartite.note: Porter collapses the name-play jokotoba into a simple simile ('modest as the creeping spray... which hides beneath the grass'), losing the wordplay-generated pivot; the shimo wish becomes a direct plea ('wander with me to-day') rather than a secret nocturnal visit, so the original name-driven wordplay pivot is replaced with a straightforward comparison-plus-invitation structure — a displaced relationship type rather than the source's lexical pivot.

kakekotoba_handling.note: Porter keeps the place name literally (Mount Ōsaka) but gives no hint of the 'meeting hill' secondary meaning; the pun's foreshadowing of union is entirely lost, so only the primary toponymic reading survives.

The vine is rendered as 'the little creeping spray... which hides beneath the grass,' a purely botanical/visual image; neither the さ寝 (sleeping together) pun nor the くる/繰る (drawing-in) association is present — the modesty/hiding is repurposed as a simile for the beloved's own modesty, not the vine's function as pivot.

The pivotal くる (come/draw-in) is not rendered as 'come' at all; instead Porter substitutes an entirely new imperative 'Wander with me to-day,' which invents a new (weaker) double sense of invitation/movement rather than preserving either the 来る or 繰る meaning of the original pivot.

kigo_handling.note: Since the source analysis marks kigo as 'none' (sanekazura carries no seasonal weight), there is no season to preserve; Porter's 'creeping spray' hidden 'beneath the grass' is a generic naturalistic image with no seasonal marking, consistent with the source's non-seasonal treatment.

entries.content_summary: Comparison introduced: 'thou art as modest as' — reworks 名にしおはば's conditional 'if the name holds true' into a direct simile addressed to the beloved.
'The little creeping spray' — renders さねかづら as a physical vine image, moved forward out of its jokotoba position.
'Upon Mount Ōsaka, which hides' — the place name 逢坂山 relocated after the vine image; 'which hides' begins to describe the vine's concealment.
'Beneath the grass; then, pray,' — completes the hiding image (vine hidden in grass) and pivots into the plea, loosely echoing 人にしられで (unknown to others).
'Wander with me to-day' — stands in for くるよしもがな, the wish that the beloved come, but reframed as a mutual outing rather than a secret nocturnal visit.

line_mapping.structural_note: Porter reorders the ku (moving the vine image before the place name) and converts the jokotoba/kakekotoba preface into a direct simile ('as modest as...'), compressing and reshuffling the kami's three ku into two lines while expanding the shimo's wish into a more casual daytime invitation, losing the secrecy and night-visit connotation of 人にしられでくる.

Porter.translator_strategy: Porter prioritizes a smooth, singable English quatrain-plus-refrain with rhyme and simile over preserving the original's wordplay, converting the name-driven kakekotoba/jokotoba into a straightforward comparison ('modest as the creeping spray') and turning the secret-meeting wish into an open daytime invitation.

bipartite.note: McCauley preserves the two-part structure (conditional preface on the name, then wish) but compresses the jokotoba into a much shorter epithet 'Trailing vine of Meeting Hill' rather than fully rendering the sanekazura-vine imagery and the 逢坂山 place-name pun with its own line; the pivot くる is rendered directly as 'draw thee to my side,' collapsing the two-step associative logic (vine one draws in → person who comes) into a single verb applied directly to the beloved, so the wordplay chain is compressed rather than fully mapped.

kakekotoba_handling.note: McCauley translates the place name transparently as 'Meeting Hill,' foregrounding the 逢 (meeting) pun but losing the sense that this is also a real, specific toponym (逢坂山/Osakayama) functioning as a place name in its own right — so only the secondary/associative meaning survives, not the literal place-name reading.
The vine is rendered literally as 'Trailing vine,' preserving the plant-name/vegetal image but dropping the さ寝 (sleeping together) pun entirely; no intimacy-connotation survives in this phrase.

'Draw thee to my side' cleverly gestures at 繰る (to draw/reel in, echoing the vine) while ultimately meaning 来る (come to me); this is the closest McCauley comes to a bilingual pun, since 'draw' can evoke pulling a vine AND the desired action of bringing the beloved near — but it's applied directly to the beloved (a person, not a vine), so the vine's own drawing action is not literally rendered, making this primary_only with a strong echo rather than full bilingual pun.

kigo_handling.note: No seasonal imagery or atmosphere survives; 'Trailing vine' is presented as a purely botanical/emotional image tied to the wordplay, not to any seasonal association, consistent with the source analysis's judgment that this poem carries no real kigo.

entries.content_summary: If thy name be true — conditional opening on 名にしおはば
Trailing vine of 'Meeting Hill' — compresses 逢坂山 and さねかづら into one line
Is there not some way — renders よしもがな (wish for a way), reordered before the secrecy clause
Whereby, without ken of men — renders 人にしられで (unknown to others)
I can draw thee to my side — renders くる (来る/繰る pivot) as the wished-for action

line_mapping.structural_note: Ku2 (逢坂山) and ku3 (さねかづら) are compressed into a single line 2 ('Trailing vine of Meeting Hill'), and the shimo's よしもがな (ku4) is split across lines 3-4 with 'is there not some way' preceding 'without ken of men' — a minor reordering that places the wish-question before the secrecy clause rather than after, though this is a natural syntactic rearrangement rather than a structural inversion of kami/shimo.

McCauley.translator_strategy: McCauley aims for a compact, singable English quatrain-like rendering that preserves the surface conceit (name-play on 'Meeting Hill' and the vine) and the emotional wish, sacrificing the full double-layered punning of さねかづら and くる for clarity and meter.
